chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan Za'lan, from Abu Talib al-Qummi, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I said, 'Did God compel the servants to commit acts of disobedience?' He said: 'No.' I said, 'Then did He delegate the matter to them?' He said: 'No.' He said: I said, 'Then what?' He said: 'A grace from your Lord between the two.'

key_terms.أَجْبَرَ: Compelled, coerced — from jabr (compulsion/determinism), the theological doctrine ascribed to Ash'aris
key_terms.الْمَعَاصِي: Acts of disobedience, sins — the question asks whether God coerces humans into these
key_terms.بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ: Between the two — shorthand for 'al-amr bayn al-amrayn', the Imami middle position
key_terms.فَوَّضَ: Delegated, entrusted — from tafwid (delegation/free will), the doctrine associated with the Mu'tazila
key_terms.لُطْفٌ: Grace, kindness, divine assistance — in Imami theology, lutf is the principle by which God facilitates human choice without compelling it

ai.seo_question: Did God compel humans to sin or give them free will? What is the Shia view on jabr and tafwid?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) articulates the foundational Imami theological position on human agency, rejecting both hard determinism (jabr) — the view that God compels humans to sin — and absolute free will (tafwid) — the view that God has entirely handed over moral agency to humans. Instead, the Imam affirms a middle position: divine grace (lutf) that lies between compulsion and delegation. This position, known as 'al-amr bayn al-amrayn' (the matter between the two matters), became the cornerstone of Imami theology distinguishing it from both Ash'ari determinism and Mu'tazili libertarianism.
